l: Domain one is twenty percent of the scored content, about ten questions. It is the vocabulary domain. The exam wants you to use terms precisely and to recognise which category a business problem falls into.
Almost every question here is really the same question in disguise: given this description, what kind of learning problem is it, and which AWS service already solves it?

Start with the nesting, because the exam tests it directly. Artificial intelligence is the broad field of machines performing tasks that need human-like intelligence. Machine learning is a subset where the system learns patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses multi-layer neural networks. Generative AI is a subset of deep learning that produces new content. Each one sits inside the one before it.

Three learning types. Supervised learning trains on labelled data, where every example carries the right answer. It splits into classification, where the output is a category, and regression, where the output is a number. Fraud detection is classification. Predicting a house price is regression.

Unsupervised learning trains on unlabelled data and finds structure by itself. Clustering groups similar records, which is how customer segmentation works. Anomaly detection flags records unlike the rest. Dimensionality reduction compresses many features into fewer. The tell in a question is that nobody labelled anything.

Reinforcement learning has an agent taking actions in an environment and receiving rewards or penalties. There is no labelled dataset, only a reward signal. Robotics, game playing and real-time bidding are the usual examples.

Then the data vocabulary. A feature is an input variable. A label is the target you are predicting. Training data teaches the model, validation data tunes it, and test data measures it on examples it has never seen. Overfitting is a model that memorised the training data and fails on new data. Underfitting is a model too simple to capture the pattern at all. Bias is error from wrong assumptions, and variance is error from being too sensitive to the training sample.

Inference is using a trained model to make a prediction. Batch inference processes a large set at once and suits reporting. Real-time inference answers a single request in milliseconds and suits interactive applications. Choosing between them by latency requirement is a very common question shape.

Now the service mapping, which is where the marks actually are. Amazon SageMaker AI is the full platform for building, training and deploying your own models. If a question describes a team that wants to train a custom model on their own data, the answer is SageMaker. If it describes a team that just wants a working capability with no model work, it is one of the pre-trained services below.

Amazon Comprehend does natural language processing on text. Sentiment, entities, key phrases, language detection, and detecting personally identifiable information in documents. When a question mentions extracting meaning from text, think Comprehend.

Amazon Textract extracts text and structure from scanned documents, including tables and form fields. The confusion to watch is Textract against Rekognition. Textract reads documents. Rekognition analyses images and video for objects, faces, moderation and scenes. A scanned invoice is Textract. A photo of a car park is Rekognition.
Amazon Transcribe converts speech to text. Amazon Polly converts text to speech. They are opposites and the exam does swap them. Transcribe listens, Polly talks.

Amazon Translate does machine translation between languages. Amazon Lex builds conversational chatbots with intents and slots, and it is the engine behind Alexa. Amazon Personalize produces real-time recommendations from user interaction data, which is the managed answer to the recommendation engine question.

Amazon Augmented AI, written A2I, adds human review to machine learning predictions when confidence is low. Whenever a question asks how to get a human in the loop on low-confidence predictions, that is A2I.

Trap one, classification against regression. The tell is the output type, not the subject matter. Predicting whether a customer will churn is classification. Predicting how many days until they churn is regression. Same business problem, different output, different answer.

Trap two, supervised against unsupervised. Ask one question: did somebody label this data? If the description mentions historical outcomes, known fraud cases, or past results, it is supervised. If it mentions discovering groups or finding unusual records with no prior examples, it is unsupervised.

Trap three, SageMaker against the pre-trained services. Both can technically solve most problems, so the qualifier decides. If the question says least operational overhead, fastest to implement, or no machine learning expertise, the answer is the managed pre-trained service. If it says custom model, proprietary data, or full control, it is SageMaker.

Trap four, Textract against Comprehend. Textract gets the words off the page. Comprehend understands what the words mean. A pipeline often uses both, in that order, and a question about processing scanned contracts end to end may well want both.
Recall drill. Answer out loud before I do. Question one. A bank wants to group customers into segments it has not defined in advance. What learning type?
Unsupervised learning, specifically clustering. Nothing was labelled, and the groups are being discovered rather than predicted.
Question two. Which service turns a scanned purchase order into structured fields, and which one would tell you the sentiment of a customer email?
Textract for the scanned document, Comprehend for the sentiment.
Question three. A model scores ninety nine percent on training data and sixty percent on new data. What is happening, in one word?
Overfitting. It memorised the training set instead of learning the pattern.
Question four. A team needs recommendations personalised per user, updated in real time, and they have no machine learning engineers. Which service?
Amazon Personalize. The no-expertise qualifier rules out building it on SageMaker.
Question five. Predicting the number of support tickets next month. Classification or regression?
Regression. The output is a number, not a category.

Carry this in. Output type decides classification against regression. Labelled data decides supervised against unsupervised. And the qualifier decides SageMaker against a managed service, every single time.
Next episode: domain two, the fundamentals of generative AI, and the twenty four percent that sits on top of everything here.
Domain two is twenty four percent, about twelve of your fifty scored questions. Together with domain three it is more than half the exam, so this is the centre of gravity.
The examiner is testing whether you understand what a foundation model is, what it costs, what it cannot do, and which AWS service you reach for. Not how transformers work internally.

A foundation model is a large model pre-trained on a broad corpus that can be adapted to many tasks. The point is generality. One model does summarisation, classification, extraction and drafting, with no task-specific training. A large language model is a foundation model specialised to text.

Tokens are the unit of everything. Models do not see words, they see tokens, which are word fragments. A rough working number is that one token is about four characters of English, so a hundred tokens is roughly seventy five words. This matters because you are billed per token, both input and output, and because the context window is measured in tokens.

The context window is how much the model can consider at once, prompt plus response together. Everything the model knows about your specific situation has to fit in there. A model does not remember previous conversations unless you resend them, which is why chat applications resend the history every turn and why long conversations get expensive.

Embeddings are the other core idea. An embedding turns text into a vector of numbers where semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness. Text meaning the same thing lands near itself even with no shared words. That is what makes semantic search work, and it is the foundation of retrieval augmented generation. A vector database stores embeddings and answers nearest neighbour queries.

Then the failure modes, which the exam does test. Hallucination is the model producing fluent, confident, false output. It is not a bug you can patch. It is a property of a system trained to produce plausible continuations, and you manage it with grounding, citation and human review rather than eliminating it. Knowledge cutoff means the model knows nothing after its training date. Non-determinism means the same prompt can give different answers, controlled by the temperature setting: low temperature is focused and repeatable, high temperature is varied and creative.

Amazon Bedrock is the answer to most questions in this domain. It is a fully managed service giving API access to foundation models from several providers, including Amazon Nova, plus Anthropic, Meta, Mistral and others, through one interface. It is serverless. There is no infrastructure to manage, and your prompts are not used to train the base models.

Understand what Bedrock includes, because it is no longer just a model endpoint. Knowledge Bases implement retrieval augmented generation as a managed capability. Agents let a model call tools and complete multi-step tasks. Guardrails filter harmful content and block denied topics. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supports running agents in production. Model Evaluation compares models on your own data.
Amazon Nova is the Amazon family of foundation models available through Bedrock, spanning text and multimodal use.

The service you most need to separate from Bedrock is Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. JumpStart gives you pre-trained models you deploy to your own SageMaker endpoints, which means you control and pay for the infrastructure. Bedrock is serverless and pay per token. The discriminator is operational overhead and control: no infrastructure means Bedrock, full control over the deployment means JumpStart.

Amazon Q is the AI assistant layer. Amazon Q Developer helps with code and AWS tasks. Amazon Q Business answers questions over your enterprise content. When a question describes an out-of-the-box assistant rather than something being built, think Q.

Trap one, Bedrock against SageMaker. Both serve foundation models. Bedrock is managed and serverless and billed per token. SageMaker means you own endpoints, instances and scaling. The qualifier decides, and least operational overhead almost always means Bedrock.

Trap two, thinking a bigger context window replaces retrieval. It does not. Retrieval augmented generation exists so you send only relevant passages, which is cheaper, faster and more accurate than stuffing everything in. A question offering both will usually want retrieval on cost grounds.
Trap three, temperature confusion. Low temperature for factual extraction and consistency. High temperature for brainstorming and variety. Candidates reverse this under pressure.

Trap four, assuming fine tuning fixes hallucination. Fine tuning changes style, format and domain behaviour. It does not make a model truthful about facts it never saw. Grounding in retrieved sources is the answer to factual accuracy.
Recall drill. Question one. Roughly how many words is a hundred tokens?
About seventy five words of English. One token is roughly four characters.
Question two. What does an embedding actually give you?
A numeric vector where semantic similarity becomes distance, so text meaning the same thing sits close together even with no words in common.
Question three. A team wants a chatbot over their internal documents with the least possible infrastructure work. Which Bedrock capability?
Knowledge Bases, which is managed retrieval augmented generation. Agents would be the answer if it needed to take actions rather than answer questions.
Question four. Which setting do you lower to make extraction from invoices repeatable?
Temperature. Low temperature gives focused, consistent output.
Question five. Bedrock or JumpStart for a team that needs full control over the deployment and instance type?
JumpStart, on their own SageMaker endpoints. Bedrock is serverless and does not expose that control.

Carry this in. Bedrock is serverless and per token, SageMaker means you own the infrastructure. Retrieval is for accuracy and cost, fine tuning is for style and format. And hallucination is managed, never eliminated.
Next episode: domain three, applications of foundation models, the single largest domain at twenty eight percent.
Domain three is twenty eight percent, the largest single domain, about fourteen scored questions. If you only have time to prepare one domain properly, prepare this one.

Nearly every question reduces to one decision: given this requirement, do you use prompt engineering, retrieval augmented generation, fine tuning, or an agent? Get that decision tree solid and you have the domain.
Take the four options in order of cost, because that ordering is the answer to most questions.

Prompt engineering is cheapest. You change the words you send. Zero shot means asking with no examples. Few shot means including a handful of worked examples in the prompt so the model infers the pattern. Chain of thought means asking the model to reason step by step, which measurably helps on multi-step problems. Prompt engineering costs nothing but tokens and takes minutes.

Retrieval augmented generation is next. You keep the model unchanged and change what you put in front of it. Documents are chunked, embedded and stored in a vector store. At query time the system embeds the question, retrieves the closest chunks, and puts them in the prompt as context. This is the answer whenever the requirement involves current information, private company data, or citations back to a source. It also reduces hallucination, because the model is answering from supplied text rather than memory.

Fine tuning is next in cost. You continue training the model on your own labelled examples so it changes behaviour permanently. It is the right answer for consistent tone, a specific output format, or specialised domain language. It requires curated training data, takes time, and produces a model you must then host. It does not teach facts reliably, and facts that change will go stale again.
Continued pre-training goes further still, training on large volumes of unlabelled domain text. Rare on this exam except as the most expensive option.

Agents are a different axis rather than a step up in cost. An agent uses a model to decide which tools to call, in what order, to complete a task. The tell in a question is action rather than answer: booking something, updating a record, calling an API, orchestrating several steps.

On AWS these map cleanly. Prompt engineering is just how you call the Bedrock API. Retrieval augmented generation is Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which handles chunking, embedding, storage and retrieval as a managed capability. Fine tuning and continued pre-training are Bedrock custom models, or SageMaker if you want full control. Agents are Amazon Bedrock Agents, with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for running them in production.
For the vector store behind retrieval, the in-scope options include Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Aurora and Amazon Neptune. OpenSearch is the common default for vector search.

Bedrock Guardrails apply content filters, denied topics, and sensitive information filtering to both the prompt and the response. When a question asks how to stop a model discussing a competitor or leaking personal data, Guardrails is the answer.
Bedrock Model Evaluation compares candidate models on your own data with automatic metrics or human review. When a question asks how to choose between models objectively, that is the service.
Amazon Augmented AI, A2I, is still the answer for routing low-confidence output to human reviewers.

Trap one, and it is the most common on the whole exam. Fine tuning offered as the fix for out-of-date or private information. It is wrong. Fine tuning changes behaviour, not knowledge. If the requirement mentions current data, internal documents, or anything that changes, the answer is retrieval augmented generation.

Trap two, the reverse. Retrieval offered as the fix for tone or output format. Also wrong. If every response must follow a strict structure or a house voice, retrieval will not do it reliably. That is fine tuning.

Trap three, reaching for the expensive option. When two answers both work, the qualifier decides, and this exam favours the cheapest thing that satisfies the requirement. Try prompt engineering first, then retrieval, then fine tuning. If a question mentions limited budget, limited data or a short timeline, move down that list, not up.

Trap four, agents against retrieval. Answering a question from documents is retrieval. Doing something in another system is an agent. If the requirement contains a verb that changes state, it is an agent.

Trap five, forgetting that these combine. A production assistant often uses retrieval for grounding, guardrails for safety, and an agent for actions. A multiple response question may well want all three.
Recall drill. Question one. A company wants a support assistant answering from documentation that changes weekly, with citations. Which approach?
Retrieval augmented generation, using Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Weekly change and citations both rule out fine tuning.
Question two. Responses must always follow the same clinical report structure. Which approach?
Fine tuning. That is consistent format and behaviour, which retrieval cannot guarantee.
Question three. The assistant must check inventory and place an order. Which approach?
An agent, because it takes actions in other systems rather than answering from text.
Question four. Accuracy on a tricky multi-step reasoning task needs to improve, with no budget and no data. What do you try first?
Prompt engineering, specifically chain of thought and a few worked examples. It costs nothing.
Question five. The model must never discuss a competitor and must never echo a customer's personal information. Which capability?
Bedrock Guardrails, with denied topics and sensitive information filtering, applied to prompt and response.

Carry this in, because it is most of the domain. Facts and freshness mean retrieval. Tone and format mean fine tuning. Actions mean agents. Safety means guardrails. And when two answers both work, the cheaper one is usually right.
Next episode: domain four, responsible AI, fourteen percent and some of the cheapest marks on the exam.

Domain four is fourteen percent, about seven scored questions. Engineers routinely under-prepare it because it feels soft, and that is a mistake. It is mostly vocabulary and judgement, there is very little to memorise, and seven questions is the difference between passing and not.
The examiner wants to know that you can name the risk, name the mitigation, and name the AWS feature that implements it.

Start with bias, because the exam distinguishes several kinds. Data bias is training data that does not represent the population it will serve. Sampling bias is collecting from an unrepresentative slice. Historical bias is data faithfully recording past discrimination, so a model trained on it reproduces that discrimination while looking accurate. Measurement bias is a proxy variable that does not mean what you assumed. Algorithmic bias arises from the model or objective itself.

Fairness is the goal, and the exam expects you to know it is contested. Demographic parity means outcomes are distributed equally across groups. Equal opportunity means the true positive rate is equal across groups. These definitions can conflict mathematically, so you cannot satisfy all of them at once, and choosing which one applies is a business and legal decision, not a technical one.

Transparency and explainability are separate ideas. Transparency is being open about the fact that AI is in use, what data it used, and what its limits are. Explainability is being able to say why a particular decision came out the way it did. A model can be transparent and still not explainable.

Interpretability against performance is a genuine trade-off the exam tests. A decision tree is interpretable and often less accurate. A deep neural network is more accurate and effectively opaque. In regulated settings, an interpretable model that you can defend often beats a more accurate one you cannot.

The other terms worth knowing precisely. Robustness is behaving sensibly on unexpected or adversarial input. Toxicity is harmful generated content. Human in the loop means a person reviews before a decision takes effect. Human on the loop means a person monitors and can intervene. Veracity is truthfulness of output, which is where hallucination lands.

The tooling maps tightly, and this is where the marks are. SageMaker Clarify detects bias in data and models and produces feature importance explanations. When a question asks how to detect bias before training or explain a prediction after it, that is Clarify.

SageMaker Model Monitor watches deployed models for drift. Data drift is the input distribution changing. Concept drift is the relationship between input and outcome changing. Both degrade a model silently, which is why monitoring is the answer to any question about accuracy declining over time after deployment.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is the generative AI control point: content filters across categories like hate and violence, denied topics you define, word filters, and sensitive information filtering that can block or mask personal data. It applies to both the prompt and the response, which matters because a user can put personal data into a prompt just as a model can put it into a reply.
Amazon Augmented AI, A2I, is the human in the loop mechanism. Low-confidence predictions get routed to human reviewers.

AWS AI Service Cards are the documentation artifact. They describe intended use cases, limitations and responsible design choices for AWS AI services. When a question asks where to find documented limitations of a service, that is the answer.
SageMaker Model Cards record a model's purpose, training data, evaluation and risk rating for governance. Model Cards document your model, Service Cards document the AWS service.

Trap one, Clarify against Model Monitor. Clarify is bias and explainability. Model Monitor is drift after deployment. The tell is whether the question is about fairness or about degradation over time.
Trap two, assuming removing a sensitive attribute removes bias. It does not. Proxy variables like postcode carry the same signal. A question offering that as a fix is offering a distractor.
Trap three, Service Cards against Model Cards. Service Cards are AWS documentation about AWS services. Model Cards are your documentation about your model.
Trap four, treating guardrails as a fix for accuracy. Guardrails block harmful and off-topic content. They do not make the model truthful. Veracity is a grounding problem.
Recall drill. Question one. A hiring model trained on ten years of past hiring decisions reproduces past under-hiring of a group. Which bias?
Historical bias. The data accurately records a biased past, so accuracy on that data is exactly the problem.
Question two. A deployed model was accurate at launch and is drifting six months later. Which service?
SageMaker Model Monitor. Drift after deployment.
Question three. You need to stop a customer service model from discussing legal advice and from echoing card numbers. Which capability?
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, using denied topics and sensitive information filtering, applied to prompt and response.
Question four. A regulator asks why one specific loan application was declined. Which capability?
SageMaker Clarify, for feature importance on an individual prediction. That is explainability rather than transparency.
Question five. Transparency or explainability: telling users that an AI system is being used at all?
Transparency. Explainability is about why a specific decision came out that way.
Carry this in. Clarify for bias and explanations, Model Monitor for drift, Guardrails for generative AI safety, A2I for humans in the loop. And removing the sensitive column never removes the bias.
Next episode: domain five, security, compliance and governance, the last fourteen percent.
Domain five is fourteen percent, about seven scored questions. Much of it is ordinary AWS security applied to AI workloads, so if you already know IAM and KMS you are most of the way there.
What is specific to this exam is data governance for training data, and the question of who owns responsibility for what.

Start with the shared responsibility model, because it frames everything. AWS is responsible for security of the cloud, meaning the infrastructure, the physical facilities and the managed service itself. You are responsible for security in the cloud, meaning your data, your access control, your encryption choices and your configuration. For a managed service like Bedrock, AWS runs the model infrastructure and you remain responsible for what you send it, who can call it, and what you do with the output.
Least privilege is the governing principle for access. Grant the minimum permissions needed, scoped to specific resources, and prefer roles over long-lived credentials.

Encryption comes in two states and the exam expects both. At rest means stored data, handled by KMS keys on S3, on SageMaker volumes and on model artifacts. In transit means data moving over the network, handled by TLS. A complete answer usually needs both.

For data governance, the vocabulary matters. Data lineage is where data came from and how it was transformed. Data cataloguing is inventorying and describing it. Data retention is how long you keep it and when it is deleted. Data residency is which geographic region it is stored and processed in, which is a common driver in regulated questions.

Two ideas specific to generative AI. First, your prompts and completions in Bedrock are not used to train the base foundation models. Second, prompt injection is an attack where user input manipulates the model into ignoring its instructions, and the mitigations are input validation, guardrails, and never granting the model more authority than the user has.

IAM controls who can call what. For AI workloads that means which principals can invoke a model, which can create training jobs, and which can read the training bucket. Roles for services, users and federation for people.

AWS Key Management Service manages encryption keys. Customer managed keys are the answer whenever a question demands control over key rotation, key policy, or the ability to revoke access by disabling a key.

Amazon Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data in S3, which is the answer to finding personal data sitting in a training dataset. Note the split against Bedrock Guardrails: Macie finds sensitive data at rest in storage, Guardrails filters it in prompts and responses at runtime.

Amazon Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities. AWS Secrets Manager stores and rotates credentials and API keys, and is the correct answer to any question where a key is hardcoded in application code.

For audit and compliance: AWS CloudTrail records who called which API and when, which is your audit trail for model invocations. Amazon CloudWatch handles metrics, logs and alarms, which is monitoring rather than audit. AWS Config tracks resource configuration changes and compliance against rules. AWS Artifact is where you download AWS compliance reports such as SOC and ISO, which is what an auditor asks for.
For network isolation, Amazon VPC with private connectivity keeps traffic off the public internet, which regulated questions often require.
Trap one, CloudTrail against CloudWatch. CloudTrail answers who did what. CloudWatch answers how it is performing. Audit means CloudTrail, every time.
Trap two, Macie against Guardrails. Both deal with sensitive data. Macie scans stored data in S3. Guardrails filters at inference time. The tell is at rest against in flight.

Trap three, AWS managed keys against customer managed keys. If the requirement mentions controlling rotation, defining a key policy, or revoking access, it is customer managed. Default encryption is not enough for those.

Trap four, misassigning shared responsibility. Anything about physical security, hypervisors or the managed service infrastructure is AWS. Anything about your data, your permissions and your configuration is you. Questions phrase this as who is responsible, and the answer is almost always the customer for anything involving data or access.
Trap five, Artifact against Config. Artifact gives you AWS compliance documentation. Config checks your own resources against rules.
Recall drill. Question one. An auditor asks for evidence of every model invocation in the last ninety days. Which service?
AWS CloudTrail. It is the API audit trail.
Question two. You must find personal data that may be sitting in a training bucket. Which service?
Amazon Macie, which discovers and classifies sensitive data in S3.
Question three. Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for encrypting the training data you upload?
You are. Security in the cloud is the customer's, and that includes your data and your encryption choices.
Question four. An application has an API key hardcoded in source. What is the fix?
AWS Secrets Manager, which stores and rotates it so the code retrieves it at runtime.
Question five. A regulator requires that you be able to revoke access to encrypted model artifacts immediately. Which key type?
A customer managed KMS key, because you can disable it and control its policy.

Carry this in. CloudTrail for who did it, CloudWatch for how it is doing, Config for configuration compliance, Artifact for AWS reports. Macie at rest, Guardrails in flight. And when a question asks who is responsible for data, it is you.
That is the five domains. The last episode in this series is a rapid service discriminator drill, which is the highest yield revision you can do the night before.
This is episode one of the AWS Certified AI Practitioner series. Before any content, you need the shape of the exam, because how it is weighted should decide how you spend your study time.

This is a foundational exam. The target candidate has up to six months of exposure to AI on AWS and uses AI solutions rather than building them. That matters, because it tells you how deep any question can go. If a question seems to demand that you tune a hyperparameter or write training code, you have misread it. That work is explicitly out of scope.

Start with the numbers. The exam has sixty-five questions. Fifty of them are scored. Fifteen are unscored trial questions that AWS is evaluating for future exams, and they are not marked or identified in any way. So roughly one question in four does not count, and you cannot tell which. The practical consequence: do not spiral on a question that feels bizarre or unfairly specific. There is a real chance it is not being scored at all.

Scoring runs from one hundred to one thousand, and you need seven hundred to pass. It is compensatory, which means you do not need to pass each domain individually. You only need to pass overall. So a weak domain can be carried by strong ones, and the right strategy is to maximise total marks rather than to even out your weaknesses.

There are four question types. Multiple choice, with one right answer and three distractors. Multiple response, where you pick two or more from five or more options and get credit only if you select every correct one and no incorrect ones. Ordering, where you place three to five steps in sequence. And matching, where you pair a list of responses against three to seven prompts. The last three types are all or nothing. Partial credit does not exist.

Unanswered questions score as incorrect and there is no penalty for guessing, so leave nothing blank. On a multiple response question where you are certain of two answers and unsure of a third, remember that adding a wrong one costs you the whole question, exactly as leaving a right one out does.

Now the five domains and their weights, because this is your study budget. Domain one, Fundamentals of AI and ML, is twenty percent. Domain two, Fundamentals of GenAI, is twenty four percent. Domain three, Applications of Foundation Models, is twenty eight percent. Domain four, Guidelines for Responsible AI, is fourteen percent. Domain five, Security, Compliance, and Governance, is also fourteen percent.

Turn those into questions. Of the fifty scored questions, domain three is about fourteen of them, domain two about twelve, domain one about ten, and domains four and five about seven each. Domains two and three together are more than half the exam. That is the generative AI half, and it is where your time should go.

One more thing that shapes your preparation. AWS publishes an in-scope service list, and it is more current than most study material. Amazon Nova, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Kiro, Strands Agents and AWS Transform are all in scope now. If your course was recorded a year ago, it will not mention several of these. Check the published list rather than trusting a video.

The first trap is depth. This exam rewards breadth. Candidates from an engineering background over-prepare on model internals and under-prepare on responsible AI and governance, which together are twenty eight percent, the same weight as the single largest domain. Those two domains are mostly vocabulary and judgement, and they are the cheapest marks on the paper.

The second trap is stale service knowledge. Questions are written against the current service catalogue. If you learned that Amazon Bedrock is only a model API, you will miss questions about agents, knowledge bases and guardrails.

The third trap is reading past the qualifier. Exam questions turn on one word: the cheapest option, the least operational overhead, the fastest to implement, the most secure. Four options can all technically work, and only one satisfies the qualifier. When you are stuck between two answers, go back and find the qualifier. It is always there, and it is usually the discriminator.

The fourth trap is the multiple response question where you know two answers and guess a third. If you genuinely cannot tell how many are correct, count the options: five options usually means two correct, and seven usually means three.
Recall drill. I will ask, you answer out loud, then I will confirm. Question one. How many questions on the exam are scored, and how many are not?
Fifty scored, fifteen unscored, sixty five in total.
Question two. What is the passing score, and do you need to pass every domain?
Seven hundred out of one thousand, and no. The scoring is compensatory, so only the overall total matters.
Question three. Which two domains together make up more than half the exam?
Domain two, Fundamentals of GenAI at twenty four percent, and domain three, Applications of Foundation Models at twenty eight percent. Fifty two percent between them.
Question four. On a multiple response question, what happens if you select three correct answers out of four correct ones?
You get nothing. Every one of these question types is all or nothing.

Three things to carry in. Seven hundred to pass, compensatory scoring, so play for total marks. Domains two and three are fifty two percent, so that is where the study time goes. And find the qualifier in every question, because it is the discriminator when several answers look right.
Next episode: domain one, the fundamentals of AI and machine learning, and the vocabulary the exam expects you to use precisely.
This is the revision episode. It cuts across all five domains and it is built for the night before, or the taxi on the way in.

Certification questions rarely ask what a service does. They give you four services that could all plausibly work and make you pick. So this episode is nothing but discriminators: pairs of services that get confused, and the single line that separates them. Play it at higher speed once you know it.

Text and documents first. Amazon Textract gets words and structure off a scanned page. Amazon Comprehend understands what text means. Scanned invoice, Textract. Sentiment of a review, Comprehend. A pipeline over scanned contracts usually needs both, Textract then Comprehend.
Speech. Amazon Transcribe is speech to text. Amazon Polly is text to speech. Transcribe listens, Polly talks.

Vision. Amazon Rekognition analyses images and video, for objects, faces, moderation and scenes. If the input is a photo or a video, it is Rekognition. If the input is a document that happens to be an image, it is Textract.

Conversation. Amazon Lex builds a chatbot you design, with intents and slots. Amazon Q is a ready-made assistant over your content or your AWS environment. Building the bot means Lex, buying the assistant means Q.
Recommendations. Amazon Personalize is the managed recommendation service. If the question says recommendations and no machine learning expertise, that is the answer, not SageMaker.

Now the generative AI pairs, which carry the most marks. Amazon Bedrock is serverless foundation model access billed per token. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart deploys models to endpoints you own and pay for. Least operational overhead means Bedrock, full infrastructure control means JumpStart.

Within Bedrock. Knowledge Bases is managed retrieval augmented generation, for answering from your documents. Agents is for taking actions across systems. Guardrails is for blocking topics and filtering sensitive data. Model Evaluation is for choosing objectively between models. Answering means Knowledge Bases, doing means Agents.

Adaptation choices. Prompt engineering costs nothing, retrieval augmented generation handles facts and freshness, fine tuning handles tone and format, continued pre-training is the expensive last resort. Facts and freshness, retrieval. Tone and format, fine tuning. Say that one out loud twice.

Responsible AI. SageMaker Clarify is bias detection and explainability. SageMaker Model Monitor is drift after deployment. Amazon A2I is human review of low-confidence predictions. AWS AI Service Cards document AWS services, SageMaker Model Cards document your model.

Security and governance. CloudTrail is who called what, the audit trail. CloudWatch is metrics, logs and alarms, the monitoring. AWS Config is resource configuration compliance. AWS Artifact is where you download AWS compliance reports. Amazon Macie finds sensitive data at rest in S3. Guardrails filters sensitive data in flight at inference. Secrets Manager holds credentials. KMS holds encryption keys, and customer managed keys are the answer whenever control over rotation or revocation is required.

Three habits that convert knowledge into marks. First, find the qualifier before you choose. Cheapest, fastest, least operational overhead, most secure, no machine learning expertise. Four options can all work and only one satisfies the qualifier, so read for it deliberately.

Second, prefer the managed service when the qualifier is about effort, and prefer the controllable service when the qualifier is about control. That single rule resolves a surprising share of the paper.

Third, on multiple response questions, count the options. Five options usually means two correct answers, seven usually means three. And remember it is all or nothing, so a guessed extra answer costs you the whole question just as a missing one does.

One last thing on timing. Sixty five questions and fifteen of them do not count. If a question feels strangely specific or unlike anything you studied, flag it, answer something, and move on. It may well be one of the unscored fifteen, and it is never worth five minutes.
Rapid drill. Answer before I do. Textract or Comprehend for pulling line items out of a scanned receipt?
Transcribe or Polly for reading a news article aloud in an app?
Bedrock or JumpStart when the requirement says no infrastructure to manage?
Bedrock. Serverless, per token.
Retrieval or fine tuning for a policy document that is revised every quarter?
Retrieval. Facts and freshness.
Retrieval or fine tuning for making every response follow the same report template?
Fine tuning. Tone and format.
Clarify or Model Monitor when accuracy has fallen six months after launch?
Macie or Guardrails for personal data already sitting in a training bucket?
CloudTrail or CloudWatch when an auditor wants a record of every model invocation?
CloudTrail. Who called what.
Lex or Q when the team wants an assistant over internal documents with nothing to build?
And last. A model must check stock levels and place a reorder. Retrieval or agent?
Agent. It takes an action rather than answering a question.
Four lines to carry into the room. Facts and freshness, retrieval. Tone and format, fine tuning. Actions, agents. Safety, guardrails.
And the meta rule that beats any individual fact: find the qualifier, then pick the cheapest option that satisfies it. Good luck.

This series is about understanding a market while it is still being built. Not about what to buy. I am not qualified to tell you that and I am not going to try. What I want, by the end, is that you can read any headline about agentic AI and judge it yourself.

Start with the honest position. Almost every number in this space is contested. Different analysts put the twenty twenty six agentic AI market anywhere from about seven billion to about eleven billion dollars, because they draw the boundary in different places. When someone quotes you a market size with no definition attached, that is a marketing number, not a measurement.

Here is what is reasonably solid. Venture funding into agentic AI companies was about six point four billion dollars across twenty twenty five, the largest year on record for the category. Through April twenty twenty six it had already reached about two point seven billion, against roughly one point one billion in the same window a year earlier.

But the shape changed more than the total. Average round size for agentic startups closing in late twenty twenty five and early twenty twenty six was about one hundred and fifty five million dollars, roughly double the eighty two million average of the first half of twenty twenty five. Fewer companies, much bigger cheques. That is a market consolidating, not a market opening up.

On adoption, Gartner projects that forty percent of enterprise applications will include task-specific agents by the end of twenty twenty six, up from under five percent in twenty twenty five. That is the number you see in every vendor deck.

And here is the number you rarely see next to it. Roughly four in five enterprises have adopted AI agents in some form, but only about one in nine is running them in production. Hold those two together. Enormous adoption, tiny production deployment.

For scale against the infrastructure spend: Morgan Stanley estimates the five largest hyperscalers will spend around eight hundred billion dollars on capital expenditure in twenty twenty six, up from about two hundred and sixty billion in twenty twenty four. The entire agentic software market is roughly one percent of what is being spent on the infrastructure beneath it.
That gap between four in five and one in nine is the most useful thing in this episode, so let me explain what causes it rather than just quoting it.

A demo agent and a production agent are different products. A demo needs to work once, in front of a friendly audience, on a happy path. A production agent needs to work on the tenth thousand attempt, on inputs nobody anticipated, with an audit trail, inside a permission model, with a defined behaviour when it is unsure. Most of the engineering is in that second list, and none of it is in the demo.

So the pilot succeeds and the rollout stalls. Not because the model got worse, but because the parts that were never built become load-bearing the moment real volume arrives. This is why enterprise AI has such a strange texture right now: genuine enthusiasm, genuine spending, and remarkably little in production.

Which gives you a lens for the whole sector. When you read that a company has some number of enterprise customers, the question is not how many. It is how many are in production, and what happens when the agent is wrong.
The strongest bear case on this specific point is not that agents do not work. It is that the production gap never closes at the speed the spending assumes.

The argument runs like this. The infrastructure is being built on a forecast of agent workloads that currently do not exist at scale. If the one in nine becomes one in three over several years rather than one in two within one year, then a large amount of capacity was built early against revenue that arrives late, or somewhere else, or to someone else.

The honest counter is that this is how most infrastructure build-outs have gone, including ones that turned out to be correct. Capacity ahead of demand is not automatically a mistake. It is only a mistake if the demand does not arrive before the assets have to be paid for. That timing question is the whole argument, and we spend a full episode on it later in this series.
Four things worth tracking, all public.
One. The production ratio. Whether that one in nine figure moves. It is the single cleanest measure of whether this is becoming real.
Two. Round sizes against round counts. Rising money into falling company counts means consolidation, and consolidation late in a cycle usually means the winners are already visible.
Three. Whether vendors start reporting agent revenue separately. Companies break out a line when it is good. Continued silence is information.
Four. The language shift from number of agents to number of tasks completed. The first is a vanity metric. The second is a business.
The one idea to carry: adoption and production are different numbers, and almost every disagreement about this market comes from quoting one while meaning the other.
Next episode: where the eight hundred billion dollars is actually going, and who is paying whom.

If you only ever hear the bull case you cannot evaluate anything, so this episode is entirely the bear case, argued as strongly as I can make it. I am not claiming it is right. I am claiming you should be able to state it before you dismiss it.
Three arguments, and they are technical rather than vibes. Depreciation, hidden lease liabilities, and circular revenue.

Argument one, depreciation. Hyperscalers generally depreciate AI hardware over five to six years. Critics argue the economic life of a leading-edge accelerator under continuous load is closer to two or three years, because it is superseded rather than because it fails. One analysis puts the resulting understatement of true asset depletion at roughly one hundred and seventy six billion dollars between twenty twenty six and twenty twenty eight.

Why that matters mechanically: depreciation is subtracted from profit. Stretch the schedule and reported earnings rise today, with the shortfall arriving later. Nobody is alleging anything improper. The schedules are disclosed. The argument is that the assumption is wrong, and that a wrong assumption compounds.

Argument two, leases. Moody's reported in early twenty twenty six that hyperscalers hold roughly six hundred and sixty two billion dollars in data centre lease commitments that are signed but not yet commenced. Under current accounting a lease does not appear on the balance sheet until it begins. So these are real, contracted obligations that a casual reading of the balance sheet does not show.

Argument three, circularity. Goldman Sachs analyst Jim Covello, the most prominent sceptic, argued in mid twenty twenty six that the industry had moved further from justifying this spending than it was two years earlier. The circularity concern is that a cloud provider invests in an AI company, which then spends that money on cloud credits with the investor, which books it as revenue. Real cash moves, but revenue growth partly reflects the investor's own capital returning home.
There is a structural reason these three arguments cluster together rather than being separate complaints.

All three are about timing mismatches. Depreciation moves cost later than the economic reality. Uncommenced leases move obligations later than the commitment. Circular deals move revenue earlier than independent demand. Each one, on its own, is defensible accounting. Together they lean the same direction: the present looks better than the underlying economics, and the correction is deferred.

That is the actual bear thesis, and it is worth stating precisely because it is falsifiable. It does not say AI is useless. It says the reported financials of the build-out are more optimistic than the cash flows will turn out to be, and the gap closes somewhere between twenty twenty seven and twenty twenty nine.

You can hold that view and still think agents transform software. The two are not in conflict. Plenty of genuinely transformative technologies were accompanied by capital losses for the people who financed the first build-out.

There is a historical rhyme worth knowing, because it is the analogy both sides reach for. In the late nineteen nineties telecoms laid enormous quantities of fibre against forecast internet demand. The forecasts were directionally right — demand did arrive, and then some. The financing was still catastrophic for the people who funded it, because the demand arrived years after the debt was due, and the capacity was so abundant that prices collapsed.

The lesson people take from that is usually the wrong one. It is not that the sceptics were right about the technology. They were wrong about the technology. It is that being right about a technology and being right about its first financing cycle are different bets, decided by different things, on different timelines.
Now the case against the bear case, which also deserves its strongest form.

On depreciation: older accelerators do not go to landfill. They move to inference, to cheaper tiers, to smaller customers. A five year schedule for an asset whose first eighteen months are premium and whose remaining years are commodity may be closer to right than the critics allow.
On leases: signed-not-commenced commitments are disclosed in the notes. They are visible to anyone who reads them. Calling them hidden overstates it.

On circularity: the practice is real, but the measurable question is what share of revenue it represents, and for the largest providers the answer appears to be a minority. Vendor financing is also not new. It accompanied most previous infrastructure cycles, including the ones that paid off.

And the strongest counter of all is the productivity evidence. A Stanford meta-analysis in April twenty twenty six found real gains where AI is actually deployed: roughly fourteen to fifteen percent in customer support, and about twenty six percent in software development. Those are measured, not projected.
Specific, checkable things.
One. Any change to stated depreciation schedules in the annual filings. A quiet shortening would be a company agreeing with the critics.
Two. The lease commitment note, not the headline balance sheet. Watch whether signed-not-commenced grows faster than revenue.
Three. Disclosed related-party revenue. If it is a minority and shrinking as a share, the circularity argument weakens on its own terms.
Four. Whether capacity utilisation is reported at all. Sustained silence about how full the data centres are is the most informative silence in this sector.

The one idea: the bear case is not that the technology fails. It is that cost is recognised late, obligations are recognised late, and revenue is recognised early. Three timing mismatches leaning the same way.
Next episode: where value actually accrues, and why owning the model may be the weakest position in the stack.

If agents are the next application layer, the money question is which layer keeps the margin. There are three candidates: the models, the infrastructure agents run on, and the applications people actually buy.
The intuitive answer is the models, and I think the intuitive answer is probably wrong.

Two data points frame it. Anthropic reported annual recurring revenue of roughly fourteen billion dollars in early twenty twenty six, up from about one billion in late twenty twenty four, and raised at a three hundred and eighty billion dollar valuation. So the model layer is not small and is not slowing.

But look at the application layer too. Salesforce disclosed Agentforce at roughly eight hundred million dollars of annual recurring revenue, up about one hundred and sixty nine percent year on year. That is a product sold into existing enterprise relationships, running on models it does not own.

Meanwhile every major cloud has moved into the layer between the two. Amazon shipped Bedrock AgentCore with managed memory, gateway, identity, runtime, observability and policy enforcement. Microsoft added long-term memory to its Foundry agent service. Google rolled Model Context Protocol support across Vertex. None of that is model research. All of it is the plumbing that makes an agent deployable.
Here is the structural argument, and it is the reusable part of this episode.

Model access is not a moat, because your competitor can call the same endpoint the same afternoon. Anything available to everyone at the same price is a cost of doing business, not an advantage. That is not a criticism of the labs — they are extraordinary businesses — it is a statement about what their customers can defend.

So what does defend? Three things keep showing up. Proprietary data that improves with use, which a competitor cannot buy. Deep workflow fit, where the product encodes how a specific industry actually operates, in its integrations and its edge cases and its compliance behaviour. And switching cost, where replacing the thing means re-training people and re-wiring systems.

Notice that all three are old-fashioned. None of them are about AI. AI amplifies an existing moat far more reliably than it creates a new one, which is why incumbent vertical software has done better through this than most people predicted.

The infrastructure layer earns its position differently. It wins by being where the agent runs — memory, identity, permissions, observability. Whoever controls the environment an agent operates in has a durable position, because moving an agent's runtime is much harder than switching its model.

Make that concrete. Picture two companies selling an agent that handles insurance claims. One wraps a foundation model in a clean interface. The other has fifteen years of claims data, integrations into the six systems every insurer actually runs, and knows which edge cases trigger a regulator.

Both demo about equally well. The first can be replicated in a quarter by anyone with the same API key. The second cannot be replicated at all without the data and the integrations, and its agent gets measurably better every month because every resolved claim is training signal its competitor never sees. Same underlying model. Completely different business.
The counter-argument is that this is a snapshot, and every layer is trying to eat the others.

The labs are moving up the stack into applications, which is exactly what you would do if you believed the application layer captures the value. The clouds are moving into the agent runtime. The application vendors are building their own orchestration to avoid depending on either.

And there is a genuine unresolved question about the orchestration frameworks specifically. The popular agent frameworks are widely used and mostly open source, and it is not settled whether that position converts into revenue or stays a commodity that the clouds absorb. Being essential and being profitable are different things.
So treat the three-layer model as a lens rather than a map. The layers are real; the boundaries are moving.

One. Whether application companies disclose gross margin separately for AI features. Thin margins mean they are passing inference costs through and have no pricing power. Healthy margins mean they are selling an outcome, not a model.
Two. Whether the labs' revenue mix shifts from API to first-party products. That tells you where they think the value is, and they have better information than you do.
Three. Whether agent runtime becomes a stated procurement decision. The moment enterprises evaluate agent infrastructure the way they evaluate a database, that layer has become durable.

And one question worth asking about any agentic product, which cuts through most pitches: what does this company have that a well-funded team with the same model access could not rebuild in six months? If the honest answer is nothing, you are looking at a feature, not a company.

The one idea: everyone can rent the same intelligence, so intelligence is not the moat. Data you uniquely have, workflows you uniquely fit, and switching costs you have earned are the moat — same as they were before any of this.
That is the series. Three episodes, and the point of all three is the same: get the mechanism, and you can price the next headline yourself.

c: Why it is built that way
l: We are reading the source of OpenAI's Codex command line agent. It is open source under Apache two point zero, it is what a serious coding agent looks like in production, and it is written in Rust across roughly a hundred crates.

The question for this episode is the most basic one. What is an agent, structurally? Because the answer you get from tutorials is: a loop that calls a model, and if the model asks for a tool, run the tool and loop again. That is about twenty lines. Let us see what the real thing looks like.

Start with scale, because it reframes everything. The core crate is around three hundred and fifteen thousand lines. The terminal interface is another two hundred and forty six thousand. The piece that most tutorials call the agent — send messages, get a tool call, execute, repeat — is a small fraction of one percent of that.

So what is the rest? Look at what sits beside the turn logic in the core crate. There are dedicated modules for context management, for compaction, for sandboxing, for execution policy, for approvals, for rollout and history, for hooks, for skills and plugins, for multi-agent delegation, for elicitation — that is asking the user a question mid-turn — and for guardians.

A turn itself is not one function. In the session module there is a turn implementation of about twenty seven hundred lines, and reading its function names tells you the shape: capture a step context, build a world state, run pre-sampling compaction, run the sampling request, stream assistant text deltas through a parser, handle plan segments, drain in-flight work, and run post-turn hooks. Cancellation tokens are threaded through all of it.
And the tool call path is separate again, with its own router, registry, orchestrator, and a parallel executor that runs tool calls concurrently with abort-on-drop handles and per-call timing.
Here is the thing worth internalising. The naive loop is not wrong, exactly. It is what remains after you delete every part that deals with reality.

Reality one: turns get cancelled. A user hits escape mid-tool-call. If cancellation is not designed in from the start, you get orphaned processes, half-applied edits, and a corrupted history. That is why cancellation tokens appear everywhere rather than at the top.

Reality two: the model streams. You cannot wait for a complete response before showing anything, so you need a parser that can handle partial text, decide when a segment is finished, and emit it — while more is still arriving. That is a state machine, not a variable.
Reality three: context runs out. Not occasionally, routinely, mid-task. So compaction cannot be an error path. It runs before sampling, as a normal part of the turn.
Reality four: tools have side effects on a real machine. Which means permission, sandboxing, and audit are not features layered on top. They are in the call path.
Put those together and the structure stops looking like over-engineering. Each subsystem exists because a specific thing goes wrong without it.

There is a fifth reality that is easy to miss, and it explains the two hundred and forty six thousand lines of terminal interface. An agent is a long-running, partially-observable process that a human has to supervise. Showing what it is doing, letting them interrupt, letting them approve — that is not decoration around the agent. For a tool people actually trust, it is a co-equal half of the product.

Notice what that implies for your own build. If you find your interface is a spinner and a wall of text at the end, you have not built a supervisable agent. You have built a batch job that happens to use a model.
So what do you actually build? Not a hundred crates. But get the shape right early, because these are the decisions that are expensive to retrofit.

Copy three things from day one. First, make the turn a state machine with explicit phases, not a while loop — even if each phase is currently trivial. Second, thread a cancellation signal through every call, before you need it. Third, treat history as an owned data structure with its own module, not as a list you append to.

Skip, for now, everything about multi-agent delegation, plugins and skills. Those are answers to problems you do not have yet, and they are the parts of this codebase most shaped by constraints specific to it.

The smallest honest version is maybe four hundred lines: a typed turn with phases, a tool registry, a cancellation token, and a history object that knows its own token count. That is a real agent. Everything after it is hardening.

One warning from the file listing. There are modules here for delegating to sub-agents, for plugins, for skills, for realtime conversation. It is tempting to read a mature codebase as a to-do list. It is not. It is the accumulated answer to years of real usage, and most of those answers are to questions you have not been asked yet.
The discipline is to copy the shape and not the surface area. Phases, cancellation, owned history. Then wait until something actually hurts before you add the module that fixes it.

The one idea: an agent is not a loop, it is a state machine wrapped in safety and context management. The loop is the part you write on the first afternoon; everything else is the part you maintain for years.
Next episode: tools, and why the interface matters far more than the implementation.

c: Why it is built that way
l: This episode is about tool design, which is where most homegrown agents go wrong. Not because the tools do the wrong thing, but because the interface the model sees is an afterthought.
Codex is unusually disciplined here, and the discipline is visible in the file layout.

In the tool handlers directory, most tools exist as a pair. There is a spec file and an implementation file, and they are separate. The planning tool has a fifty eight line spec and a hundred and five line implementation. The shell tool has a four hundred and fourteen line spec against a two hundred and fifty six line implementation.
Read that ratio again. For the shell tool, describing the interface to the model takes more code than doing the work. That is not an accident.

A spec is a function returning a tool specification: a name, a description, a JSON schema for parameters, a strictness flag, and — this is the part people miss — an optional output schema. Codex declares the shape of what a tool returns, not just what it accepts.

Tools are then registered into a registry, and the registry distinguishes trusted tools from external ones. External tools, which is largely how Model Context Protocol servers arrive, go through a separate registration path, and the registry tracks name collisions explicitly rather than letting a late registration silently shadow a built-in.
There is also a tool search tool, and specs can be marked to defer loading — because when an agent has access to hundreds of tools, putting every schema in the prompt is itself the problem.
The separation of spec from handler looks like ceremony until you notice what it prevents.

The model never sees your implementation. It sees the schema and the description, and that is the entire contract. So the quality of your agent is bounded by the quality of that description, and a description buried at the top of a function that also does the work will always be an afterthought. Put it in its own file and it becomes something you review.
Output schemas matter for the same reason in reverse. If the model knows the shape of what comes back, it can plan two steps ahead instead of calling a tool to find out what the tool returns.

The trusted-versus-external split is a security boundary. When an agent can install third-party tool servers, a malicious or careless one could register a tool named the same as your shell tool. If registration silently overwrites, you have just handed control to whatever registered last. Tracking the first collision turns a silent takeover into a visible conflict.

And deferred loading is a context-economics decision. Every tool schema in the prompt costs tokens on every single request for the entire session. Past a few dozen tools, you are paying a permanent tax to describe capabilities the model will never use in this task.

There is a second-order effect worth naming. Because the spec lives apart from the handler, you can change how a tool is described without touching what it does — and that is the highest-leverage tuning available in an agent. Most behaviour problems people try to fix with prompt engineering at the system-prompt level are really tool-description problems, one layer down.
If your agent keeps using the wrong tool, the fix is almost never a sterner system prompt. It is a clearer boundary between two tool descriptions that currently overlap.
Copy the split immediately. It costs nothing when you have three tools and it is painful to introduce when you have thirty.

Write the description as if for a competent colleague who cannot see your code and cannot ask questions. State when to use the tool, when not to, and what it returns. Most tool descriptions are a noun phrase; that is a wasted opportunity.
Declare output schemas even if your framework does not require them. It is the cheapest planning improvement available.
Namespace external tools and refuse silent collisions. Even in a personal project, the day you add someone else's tool server you will want that boundary already there.
Defer loading only when you actually have many tools. Below roughly a dozen it is complexity for nothing.

A test worth writing early: assert that no two tool descriptions could plausibly match the same request. It is a judgement call, so it is a review checklist rather than an automated test — but running it once, out loud, over your tool list will usually find one overlapping pair you had not noticed.

One more pattern from the handler list worth copying when you get there. Several tools exist purely so the model can ask for something rather than assume it: request user input, request permissions, request a plugin install. Each is a tool whose entire job is to hand control back.

That is a good instinct to build in early. When your agent hits ambiguity, the choice is not only guess or fail. A tool that asks is often the highest-value tool in the set, and it costs almost nothing to implement.
The one idea: your tool's schema is the product surface the model buys from. The implementation is just what happens after the sale.
Next episode: permissions — which in an agent that runs shell commands is not a feature but the whole design.

c: Why it is built that way
l: An agent that can run shell commands on your machine is, functionally, remote code execution that you invited in. So the interesting question is not whether it can be made safe in the abstract. It is what the safety machinery actually looks like when someone builds it seriously.
This is the episode where the code taught me the most, and where the lesson transfers furthest beyond coding agents.
Start with the central type. The safety module defines a check result with exactly three variants: auto-approve, ask the user, or reject. And reject carries a reason string.

Three values, not two. That single design choice is most of the episode. A boolean can-I-do-this forces every uncertain case into one of two bad outcomes: block something legitimate, or allow something dangerous. A third value moves the decision to the only party who can actually resolve it.

The reason string matters too, because it goes back to the model. When a patch is refused for writing outside the project, the model is told that, in those words, and can adapt. A bare denial teaches it nothing and it will try again.

Above that sits an approval policy with several levels: never ask, ask on request, ask unless trusted, and a granular mode with per-capability flags. That is a user preference, and it is separate from the per-action assessment.

Then the sandbox layer, which is entirely separate again. There is a sandboxing crate with Landlock and bubblewrap implementations, a dedicated Linux sandbox crate, and a Windows sandbox crate running to about nineteen thousand lines on its own. Sandboxing is per-platform and it is a large fraction of the total codebase.
And there is an execution policy subsystem with its own tests running to thousands of lines, which classifies commands before they run.
Now the detail I found genuinely instructive, and it is a comment in the patch safety code.

Before applying a patch, the code checks whether every path is inside a writable root. If it is, you might reasonably auto-approve and run it directly. Codex does not. It still runs the patch inside the sandbox — because a path inside a writable root could be a hard link to a file outside it.
Sit with that. The policy check passed. The paths were all legitimate. And they still assume it might be lying, because the filesystem allows an alias that the path string does not reveal.

That is defence in depth stated concretely: the policy layer and the sandbox layer are not redundant, because they fail differently. Policy reasons about intent expressed as strings. The sandbox enforces at the kernel boundary, where the string cannot lie. Either alone is bypassable; together they are not, at least not by that trick.

The other structural lesson is that the safety decision is a pure function. It takes the action, the policy, the permission profile, the sandbox policy, and the working directory, and it returns a verdict. No side effects. Which means it is exhaustively testable — and indeed the safety and policy test files run to thousands of lines. Security logic that is tangled into execution cannot be tested this way, and so in practice is not tested.

One more design property to notice: the policy levels and the per-action assessment are independent axes. The user's preference is a setting; whether this specific action is dangerous is a computation. Keeping them separate is why a granular mode is possible at all — you can turn individual capabilities on without rewriting the assessment logic.

When people conflate the two, you get the familiar bad outcome: a single yolo flag that disables all reasoning about risk, because the only place risk was considered was inside the prompt asking permission.
Three things to copy, and they are cheap.
One. Make your permission check three-valued from the first commit. Auto-approve, ask, reject-with-reason. Retrofitting the ask branch later means touching every call site.
Two. Return the reason to the model, not just to the user. An agent that is told why it was refused will route around the obstacle; one that gets a bare failure will retry the same thing.
Three. Keep the decision pure. Inputs in, verdict out, no execution. Then test it like the security control it is.

What to skip: do not write your own sandbox. Use the platform primitive — Landlock or seccomp on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS, the job and integrity primitives on Windows — or run the whole thing in a container. Nineteen thousand lines for one platform should tell you how badly this goes if you improvise it.
And do not conflate the two layers. Policy is what the user allows. Sandbox is what the kernel enforces. If your design only has one of them, you have the weaker half.

The one idea: a boolean permission check is a design bug. Three values — allow, ask, refuse with a reason — and two independent layers, because the layer that reasons about strings and the layer that enforces at the kernel fail in different ways.
Next episode: context, and why running out of it is a normal event rather than an error.

c: Why it is built that way
l: Every agent that does real work runs out of context. Not as a rare failure — routinely, in the middle of a task, on the tenth tool call. How a system handles that is most of the difference between an agent that finishes work and one that forgets what it was doing.
So this episode is about what Codex does when the window fills.

The first signal is the file listing. In the core crate there are roughly ten modules whose names begin with compact: local compaction, remote compaction, a second version of remote compaction, token-budget compaction, model fallback for compaction, and their tests. There is a separate context manager directory containing history, normalisation and updates. Context handling is not a helper function; it is a subsystem with more code than the turn loop.

Second, compaction is modelled as part of the turn lifecycle, not as an exception. The turn runs pre-sampling compaction before it ever calls the model. There are named triggers — manual, automatic, token-budget — and the analytics distinguish them, because how often each fires tells you something different about your system.
Third, there are pre-compact and post-compact hooks. External code can observe or participate when history is about to be rewritten.

Fourth, and this is the subtle one: token-budget compaction deliberately skips model summarisation and installs a fresh context window instead. The comment says it is still modelled as compaction so that hooks and turn items see the same lifecycle. Different strategy, same shape.
There is also a tool the model can call to ask how many tokens remain. The agent can reason about its own budget.
The naive approach is to summarise the conversation when it gets long. That fails in three ways this design addresses.

It fails on timing. If you compact only when a request is rejected for length, you compact under pressure, after wasting a call, and possibly mid-tool-sequence. Running compaction before sampling means the decision happens when the state is clean.

It fails on strategy. Sometimes the right move is a model-written summary. Sometimes — when a task is genuinely finished and a new one begins — the right move is to throw the window away and start fresh, which is much cheaper and loses nothing. Treating these as one operation with different strategies, rather than as unrelated code paths, is why both get the same hooks and the same audit trail.

It fails on observability. Compaction is lossy by definition. If it happens invisibly, you cannot debug the resulting amnesia — the agent forgets a constraint and you have no record of when it was dropped. Emitting compaction as an item in the turn history makes the loss inspectable.
And exposing remaining tokens to the model is a small idea with a large effect: an agent that knows it is running low can choose to summarise its own findings before they are taken from it.

Worth naming the failure mode this prevents, because it is the one people actually hit. An agent is halfway through a refactor. Context fills. Something summarises the history, and the summary keeps the plan but drops the constraint the user gave in message three — do not touch the public API. The agent continues confidently and breaks the thing it was told not to break.

No amount of model quality fixes that, because the information is gone before the model sees it. It is an architecture problem, and it is solved at the point where you decide what compaction is allowed to discard.
The smallest version that is still correct has four properties.

History is an object, not a list. It knows its own token count, and it is the only thing allowed to mutate itself. The moment several call sites append directly to an array, you have lost the ability to reason about the budget.
Compaction is checked before every model call, not after a failure. One conditional at the top of the turn.
Compaction emits an event into the history it just rewrote, so the record shows what happened.

And you have at least two strategies: summarise when the work continues, reset when it does not. You do not need remote compaction, versioned variants, or hooks until other people's code depends on yours.
One more thing worth stealing cheaply: give the model a way to ask how much room is left. It is a handful of lines and it changes how the model paces itself.

A practical note on ordering, since it catches people. Compact before you add the new user message, not after. If you compact after, the thing most likely to be summarised away is the instruction you just received — which is the single worst thing to lose and, awkwardly, the most recent.

And keep the first system message and the current task statement out of whatever gets compacted. Pin them. Almost every agent amnesia story ends with one of those two having been quietly summarised into nothing.

The one idea: context exhaustion is a normal event on the happy path. Design for it in the turn lifecycle, with history as an owned object that knows its own size — not as an error handler bolted on when you first see a length exception.
That is the series. Four episodes, one underlying message: in a production agent, the model call is the easy part. The loop, the interface, the permission model and the budget are the system.

c: Why it is built that way
l: In episode three we covered permissions: three-valued checks, sandboxes, defence in depth. There was one branch I skipped, and it is the most interesting thing in the whole repository.

When the policy says ask the user, Codex does not always ask the user. Sometimes it asks a second model instead. That subsystem is called the guardian, and it is about eight thousand eight hundred lines including tests.

The module documentation states the approach in four steps, and the fourth is the important one. Reconstruct a compact transcript preserving user intent plus recent context. Ask a dedicated guardian review session to assess the exact planned action and return strict JSON. Fail closed on timeout, execution failure, or malformed output. Apply the explicit allow or deny outcome.

So it is a separate review session, not a side question inside the main conversation. It clones the parent configuration, which means it inherits the same network proxy and allowlist the parent turn was operating under. The reviewer is not given more power than the thing it is reviewing.
